stops.name: Sochi: the sea reached, the party sifted
stops.campa: They come down out of the passes to the palms and mud of Sochi, into White-held coast, and the expedition dissolves the way his enterprises always dissolve once their real work is done: the mountain has sorted the pilgrims. Several of the oldest pupils fall away here, kept by families, fears, or their own counsel. He winters on the coast without visible regret: sells silk, doctors the sick, plans forward. The teaching travels light into 1919: Ostrowska, the de Hartmanns, the Stjernvalls, a few more. Enough.

stops.name: Tiflis, the Institute founded; the Movements take the Opera stage
stops.campa: In Tiflis, city of his railway youth, the wandering school becomes an Institution: the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man is founded here first, its prospectus as grand as its treasury is thin. The painter Alexandre de Salzmann and his wife Jeanne, mistress of a Dalcroze studio, join him; to Jeanne's trained dancers he begins to give the sacred movements carried from the Sarmoung valley. On 22 June 1919, at the Tiflis Opera House, the dances written in the hidden monastery are performed on a public stage of Europe's edge for the first time.

stops.name: Constantinople, the Institute in Pera
stops.campa: Georgia buckles, and the school ships from Batum to Constantinople, a city between two corpses of empire, swollen with White Russian refugees selling their rings on the Grande Rue. Gurdjieff sells carpets, cures nerve-cases, and within weeks has the Institute running in Pera: movements classes, lectures, the Struggle of the Magicians in rehearsal. Here a young English intelligence officer named John Bennett, watching him move through a crowded room, meets the strangest man he will ever know, and is marked for life without understanding what has touched him.

stops.name: The Mevlevi tekke at Galata, the turning explained
stops.campa: He takes Ouspensky and the pupils to the Mevlevi house at Galata, where the dervishes wheel under the wooden dome, skirts opened into white planets. The visitors see ecstasy; he shows them mathematics. The turning, he explains, is built on counting: exercises of attention hidden inside what Europe calls a dance of trance, the mind held to inner sequences while the body orbits. It is the Sarmoung lesson again, spoken in Ottoman accent: what survives of real knowledge survives disguised as worship, art, and spectacle.

stops.name: Berlin, the western foothold that would not hold
stops.campa: Kemal's war closes Anatolia and the school moves again, west into the hungry brilliance of Weimar Berlin. He lectures in Schöneberg halls, negotiates for the famous Dalcroze building at Hellerau outside Dresden, the very temple of European movement-training, which he means to capture for the sacred dances, and is balked by lawsuits and bad faith. Germany, inflation-mad, will not carry the Institute. England beckons through Ouspensky's new London following, but the Home Office bars the master himself. The compass settles on France.

stops.name: London, the visitation of Ouspensky's group
stops.campa: He descends on London in February 1922 and speaks to the group Ouspensky has built in his name, and over his head. In a Kensington drawing-room packed with editors, doctors and theosophists in recovery, the man himself, in broken and blazing English-through-interpreters, makes his pupils' careful system look like a photograph of a fire. Orage, the most brilliant editor in England, decides on the spot where his life is going. Ouspensky watches his own students turn like compass needles, and the long schism of the canon begins here, politely, over tea.

stops.name: Paris, arrival with the last of the fortune
stops.campa: He reaches Paris in the high summer of 1922 with his people, his manuscripts and the remains of a fortune worn down by five years of escaping. The Dalcroze school lends its premises; wealthy English pupils, Lady Rothermere's cheque-book at their head, gather the funds the Home Office refused him hospitality. He scouts châteaux like a general choosing ground. The city that will hold his cafés, his crashes and his deathbed receives him without ceremony, one more Russian refugee, as it thinks, among a hundred thousand.

stops.name: The Prieuré des Basses Loges, Fontainebleau-Avon: the gates open
stops.campa: On the first of October the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man takes possession of the Prieuré des Basses Loges at Avon: a prior's estate become a Dreyfus mistress's château, forty-five rooms, fountains, and a wall around a world. The regime begins at once: pupils who were lawyers and countesses dig ditches, fell trees, wash dishes into the night, and are roused before dawn; hard labor is the first language of the teaching. Madame Ostrowska rules the kitchen; the Russians and the English eat at one long table under the master's weather-making eye.

stops.name: The Study House, raised by the pupils' hands
stops.campa: A war-surplus airship hangar is bought, carted to the grounds, and in weeks of day-and-night labor the pupils raise the Study House with their own blistered hands: earth floor covered with carpets from his caravans, a perfumed fountain, painted windows, the aphorisms of the work lettered around the walls in a script devised so that only those taught to read it can. Here the Movements are drilled every evening, the dances of the Sarmoung transplanted into French winter mud, while Gurdjieff sits above on a divan, mending souls, as he says, by making bodies obey.
stops.quote_source: Aphorism inscribed in the Study House at the Prieuré

stops.name: The cowshed loft, Katherine Mansfield
stops.campa: Katherine Mansfield, the finest short-story writer in English and dying of tuberculosis, arrives in October having chosen the Prieuré over the doctors' sanatoria. Gurdjieff builds her a gallery loft above the cows, de Salzmann painting it with flowers and beasts, and prescribes the old Asian regimen: animal warmth, milk-breath, the watching of simple work. She scrapes carrots in the kitchen, watches the Movements at night, and writes last letters full of a hard new peace: she wants to be all of herself, root and branch. On the ninth of January, climbing the stairs, the hemorrhage comes; she dies within the hour and is buried at Avon.

stops.name: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées: Paris sees the sacred dances
stops.campa: From the thirteenth of December the Institute takes the stage of the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the hall of the Rite of Spring scandal, for public demonstrations of the sacred gymnastics: an orchestra of thirty-five plays the de Hartmann scores, dervish dances and temple movements succeed one another with military exactness, and in the stop exercise dancers hurl themselves at the footlights and are frozen by one word from the dark auditorium, falling and holding like statuary shot from a catapult. Paris, Diaghilev's Paris, does not know whether it has seen art, drill, or liturgy. It has seen the Sarmoung library, opened.

stops.name: New York, Carnegie Hall
stops.campa: In January he sails with thirty-five pupils on the S.S. Paris to conquer the New World, Orage sent ahead as herald. Demonstrations mount from Leslie Hall to the summit: on the third of March the sacred dances fill the main stage of Carnegie Hall. America, which measures everything, watches human beings move with a precision it cannot measure, and the harvest is exactly what he came for: the Americans, writers, editors, heiresses, the young Jean Toomer, who will fund and carry the work for the rest of his life. He returns to France in June with the dollar rope that will hold through every coming shipwreck.
